n: In this lecture we will study health impairment and deaths caused by chemical agents. Such cases are relatively common in expert practice. Among violent deaths, poisonings rank third, after mechanical injuries and mechanical asphyxia. The outline is as follows: the concept of poison and poisoning, the factors of poisoning, forensic medical diagnosis, toxicokinetics, toxicodynamics and the classification of poisons. Further on, we will consider poisoning by corrosive, destructive, blood and functional poisons.

t: The concept of poison and poisoning
n: Let us begin with the concept of poison and poisoning. Poison is a relative concept: it is a substance that, in a small amount, impairs health or causes death. There is no absolute poison, and no absolutely harmless substance. The saying of Paracelsus expresses this: only the dose turns a given substance into a medicine or a poison. Impairment of health resulting from the action of a substance in a small amount is called poisoning. In forensic medicine, a poison is a substance that, even when it enters the body in a small amount, impairs health or causes death through its chemical or physico-chemical properties.

Let us consider the branches of toxicology. They are industrial, agricultural, military, food, household and forensic toxicology. Attention: forensic toxicology is not a therapeutic science; it resolves legal questions. In the other branches the main concern is the cause and prevention, and the victim is given qualified medical care. In forensic toxicology, by contrast, the questions posed by the commissioning authorities are resolved; this is not treatment but expert examination. The development of forensic medicine as a science began with forensic toxicology.

t: Classification of poisonings: cause and circumstances
n: We shall look at the classification of poisonings by cause and circumstances. By origin, poisoning is homicidal, suicidal or accidental. In practice most cases are accidental, followed by suicide; homicidal poisoning is rare. By cause, poisoning is intentional or unintentional: suicide, homicide or mistaken ingestion. By setting, occupational, domestic and iatrogenic groups are distinguished. Iatrogenic poisoning results from an incorrectly determined drug dose or from the use of one drug instead of another.

Quick questions on the basic concepts. First question: what is a poison in forensic medicine? Answer: a substance that, in a small amount, impairs health or causes death. Second question: what is meant by poisoning? Answer: impairment of health arising from the action of a substance in a small amount. Third question: when does iatrogenic poisoning occur? Answer: with a dosing error during a medical procedure, or when one drug is substituted for another. Attention: there is a risk of error. There is no absolute poison and no absolutely harmless substance; according to Paracelsus, the dose turns a substance into a medicine or a poison.

t: Case analysis: determining the type of poisoning
n: Case analysis: we determine the type of poisoning. In the first case, workers passed off one of the reagent containers as "spirit" and drank from it at lunch. Those who drank lost consciousness and died quickly; dichloroethane was found in the corpse. In the second case, a nembutal solution was injected subcutaneously into a 15-year-old girl; after she lost consciousness and became helpless, she was raped. In intentional poisoning, a substance may also be used to render the victim helpless, that is, for robbery or rape; death is not required. Question: what is the main criterion for classifying both cases as homicide, suicide or accident: was there intent, or did the poison enter by chance?

t: Four groups of factors influencing poisoning
n: The factors influencing poisoning fall into four groups: the poisonous substance, the organism, the route of entry and external conditions. The poisonous substance factor includes dose, solubility and physical state. The organism factor includes body weight, age, health and genetics. The route-of-entry factor includes skin, mouth, respiratory tract and injection. External conditions include temperature, humidity and an enclosed environment. The faster and more completely a poison passes into the blood, the higher the degree of toxic effect. External conditions matter only for some substances: with carbon monoxide and alcohol, an enclosed, hot, humid environment creates a predisposition.

t: Factors related to the poisonous substance
n: We shall consider the factors related to the poisonous substance. Chemical structure determines the properties. Carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide both consist of carbon and oxygen, yet their toxicity is not the same. In pharmacology, therapeutic, toxic and lethal doses are distinguished. A gaseous substance acts more strongly than a liquid one, and a liquid more strongly than a solid, because it passes into the blood faster. Organophosphorus compounds dissolve readily in fats, and are therefore absorbed even through intact skin. The effect of a drug, in turn, depends on its shelf life and storage conditions.

t: Factors related to the poisonous substance (continued)
n: We continue with the factors related to the poisonous substance. The vehicle, that is, the substance that carries the poison into the body, alters the effect. For example, arsenic is enhanced in an alkaline medium, and hydrocyanic acid in an acidic one. Heavy metals accumulate in the body; this phenomenon is called cumulation. In other words, the same poison may act differently in different media and conditions.

t: Differences between poisons: solubility and concentration
n: Differences between poisons: solubility and concentration. The effect of a 3% vinegar solution cannot be compared with that of acetic essence; concentration is decisive. The example of Rasputin: potassium cyanide, stored for a long time, combined with CO2, turned into potash and lost its toxicity. Attention: corrosive sublimate is not calomel, and barium chloride is not barium sulphate. The difference is determined by solubility. Insoluble substances are harmless: barium sulphate is used in radiology as a contrast meal, and calomel is relatively harmless. Soluble substances are poisonous: barium chloride is a strong poison, and corrosive sublimate is strongly toxic.

Organism-related factors. Body mass is important: the same amount of poison does not act equally in people of different weights, which is why a drug dose is calculated per 1 kg of body weight. There is no difference between the sexes, but sensitivity increases in pregnancy. Children are more sensitive than adults: their body mass is small and their resistance system is not fully formed. A healthy organism resists more strongly; in heart, liver and kidney disease this ability is limited. The contents of the stomach alter absorption. Genetics: when cholinesterase is low, muscle relaxants act more strongly. Idiosyncrasy is hypersensitivity to certain substances.

Tolerance, abstinence, narcomania and toxicomania. Repeated action of a poison over a short period may lead to tolerance, that is, habituation: this occurs with hypnotics, analgesics and antihypertensive drugs. With narcotic substances, psychological and physical dependence develops along with tolerance: there is a drive to take more, and if the substance is not taken, an abstinence syndrome appears. Narcomania is a disease arising from the non-medical use of agents recognised as narcotics; toxicomania arises from substances not on the list. Attention: for a substance to be called a narcotic, the medical, social and legal criteria must all be met together; if one is missing, the substance is not a narcotic.

t: Routes of entry of poison and external conditions
n: Routes of entry of poison and external conditions. The routes of entry are the skin, mouth, respiratory tract, rectum and injection. The faster the poison passes into the blood, the stronger the effect. A poison entering through the respiratory tract, rectum or vagina does not pass through the liver, and therefore acts more strongly; a poison absorbed through the mucosa of the stomach and intestine passes through the liver, and its effect is weaker. Substances that dissolve well in fat, for example organophosphorus compounds, are absorbed even through intact skin. In occupational poisoning, external conditions are important; hydrogen sulphide is encountered in sewer wells. In an enclosed, hot, humid environment the effect is stronger, and in an open environment it is weaker.

Quick questions on the factors. How many groups of factors are significant in poisoning? Four: the poisonous substance, the organism, the route of entry, and the external conditions at the time of action. Why is an organophosphorus compound dangerous through the skin as well? Because it dissolves well in fat and is absorbed into the blood even through intact skin. Which route of entry gives a stronger effect? A poison absorbed through the respiratory tract, rectum and vagina does not pass through the liver, and therefore acts more strongly than one absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract. Attention: there is a risk of error! Carbon monoxide is not carbon dioxide. Both consist of carbon and oxygen, but their toxic properties are not the same.

t: Case analysis: factors and the strength of poisoning
n: Case analysis: factors and the strength of poisoning. Situation: a three-year-old child drank a small glass of vodka and died. Question: to which group of factors does this belong, and why? Answer: the age factor. Children are more sensitive than adults: their body mass is small and the general resistance system is not fully formed. On phenol: its concentrated solution causes only a local chemical burn, whereas a diluted one has a resorptive effect and damages the internal organs and brain. Another question: what if the poison gets onto the skin of a person who worked with an organophosphorus compound? Because it dissolves in fat, it passes into the blood even through intact skin.

t: Forensic medical diagnosis of poisoning: 3 stages
n: The forensic medical diagnosis of poisoning consists of three stages. The first stage: examination of the scene and review of the medical documents; physical evidence is collected. The second stage: examination of the corpse, that is, attention is paid to cadaveric lividity, odour and rigor mortis. The third stage: laboratory examination, in which the "three points" rule is applied. The expert resolves the following: whether poisoning occurred, which substance, by what route and in what dose. In other words, the conclusion rests not on a single stage but on all three together.

t: Examination of the scene and documents
n: Examination of the scene and documents. At the scene, vessels, packaging, vomit and gastric lavage fluid suspected of containing poison are collected, wrapped and sent for forensic chemical examination. Empty vessels are also taken, because poison may be found in their rinsings. Poison may be present in the vomit but absent from the internal organs. Medical documents are important: with poisons that leave no morphological changes, the clinical description and previous laboratory results become weighty evidence. Attention: there is a risk of error. A diagnosis cannot be made from a single clinical sign, for example vomiting; vomiting also occurs in head injury.

t: External and internal signs on the corpse
n: External and internal signs on the corpse. On external examination, attention is paid to staining around the mouth, the state of the pupils, the colour of the skin and the odour of the internal organs. The colour of the cadaveric lividity is also informative: bright red patches suggest carbon monoxide, and brown patches suggest methaemoglobin-forming agents. If rigor mortis is very strongly developed, strychnine is possible; a yellowish skin and conjunctiva are characteristic of haemolytic poisons. Water and antiseptic are not used during dissection, because poisonous substances may be washed away. First the heart is incised and blood is taken, then the stomach and intestines, with their ends tied off, are removed.

t: Laboratory examinations and choice of objects
n: Laboratory examinations and choice of objects. Forensic chemical examination is performed most often, and both qualitative and quantitative determination are carried out. Histological, biochemical, pharmacological, botanical and physical methods are also used. The "three points" rule: objects are taken from where the poison entered, where it mainly acted, and where it was excreted. When the poison was taken by mouth, the stomach contents, a piece of liver and a kidney with urine are taken. When the poison is unknown, 1/3 of the brain, 1/4 of the lung, 1/3 of the liver with the gallbladder, a whole kidney with urine, the stomach contents, intestine and 100–200 ml of blood are taken. Attention: finding or not finding a poison is not proof in itself; it may have passed into the corpse later, been excreted from the body, or been broken down.

Evaluation of results and exhumation. In an exhumed corpse, samples are also taken from the clothing, coffin lining, ornaments and the soil in contact with the corpse; 6 soil samples. Alcohol and potassium cyanide do not keep for long. Arsenic, heavy-metal salts and strychnine are well preserved, and so may be found even in a corpse buried for a long time. Attention: finding a poison does not always prove poisoning.

We continue with the evaluation of results. A substance may pass into the corpse after death from the external environment, from the coffin lining, or from a contaminated vessel. Therefore a positive result alone is not sufficient. A negative result, in turn, does not exclude poisoning: the substance may have been completely excreted or broken down before death; this process is called biotransformation.

Case analysis: diagnostic error. First example: a young man was brought in from the street unconscious, with a strong smell of alcohol from his mouth and traces of vomit on his clothing. The doctor, regarding it as severe alcohol poisoning, washed out his stomach. He died several hours later. At autopsy a fracture of the cranial vault and an epidural haematoma were found: the head injury had not been recognised in time. Second example: a 3-year-old girl had convulsions, with foam and blood from the mouth; internal bleeding was suspected.

We continue the example of diagnostic error. When the skull was opened, no blood was found, and amidopyrine was detected in the stomach; the girl had taken 10 tablets before the fall. Question: are vomiting, unconsciousness or the smell of alcohol alone sufficient for a diagnosis? No, because vomiting may also occur in cerebral haemorrhage. This means that the diagnosis must rest not on a single sign but on the totality of the examinations.

Toxicokinetics and toxicodynamics. Toxicokinetics is the entry, distribution, metabolism and excretion of a poison. Biotransformation takes place mainly in the liver. Toxicodynamics, in turn, is the totality of the body's responses to the poison and its metabolite. In acetic acid poisoning the primary effect is a chemical burn, the subsequent effect is haemolysis, and the metatoxic effect is toxic hepatitis and nephrosis. In oxidation, the parent substance is converted into a metabolite. The metabolite of methyl alcohol is formaldehyde, which is cardio-, nephro- and neurotoxic. The metabolite of ethyl alcohol is acetaldehyde, a more strongly toxic substance. The metabolite of ethylene glycol is oxalic acid, which is hepato- and nephrotoxic.

t: Routes of excretion of poisons and sites of accumulation
n: Routes of excretion of poisons and sites of accumulation. Poison is excreted through organs with an external secretory function: the lungs, liver, kidneys, gastrointestinal tract, skin, and the mammary and salivary glands. Volatile substances are excreted through the lungs, water-soluble ones through the kidneys, heavy metals through the large intestine, and fat-soluble ones with the bile. Narcotics and alcohol are excreted through the mammary and salivary glands. Fat-soluble substances accumulate in the brain, liver and adipose tissue; water-soluble ones in muscle, liver and kidneys. Arsenic and lead accumulate in bone and hair. Mercury accumulates in the brain, bone and kidneys. For this reason, poison can be found in a corpse even after decades.

Forensic medical classification of poisons. Poisons are divided into those acting mainly locally and those acting mainly generally. Local poisons cause necrosis at the site of contact; general poisons act after absorption into the blood, which is the resorptive effect. Corrosive poisons belong to the local group: acids, alkalis, tincture of iodine. General poisons are divided into three groups. Destructive poisons: mercury, lead, arsenic, phosphorus; they cause tissue destruction in the internal organs. Blood poisons: carbon monoxide and methaemoglobin-forming agents; they act on haemoglobin and cause hypoxia. Functional poisons: cyanides, strychnine, alcohols; they disturb the activity of the nervous system.

Quick questions on the classification. First question: to which group do acids and alkalis belong, and what change do they cause at the site of contact? Second question: to which groups of general poisons do mercury, lead, arsenic, phosphorus and cyanides belong? Answer: acids and alkalis are local poisons that cause necrosis; mercury, lead, arsenic and phosphorus are destructive; cyanides are a functional poison. Attention: there is a risk of error. A "mainly local" poison also causes a general reaction; local does not mean only local.

Corrosive poisons: acids. Acids damage through free hydrogen ions: they dehydrate tissue, coagulate protein and produce coagulative, that is, dry, necrosis. In the oesophagus and stomach there is severe pain and bloody vomit, and sometimes fragments of mucous membrane are expelled. Swelling of the larynx and spasm of the glottis are possible. In the first hours the cause of death is shock, asphyxia or internal bleeding. At a later stage the cause is pneumonia, hepatorenal failure, mediastinitis or peritonitis. Lethal dose: sulphuric and nitric acid 5–10 ml, hydrochloric acid 15–20 ml, acetic essence 20–40 ml, carbolic acid 10–30 ml.

t: Acids: signs on the corpse and differences
n: Acids: signs on the corpse and differences. Sulphuric acid is strong: the stomach wall is damaged more, and perforation is common. With sulphuric acid the eschar is brownish-black. With nitric acid it is yellowish, at concentrations above 30%; the smell of nitrogen oxide and pulmonary oedema are observed. With hydrochloric acid it is brownish-grey, and laryngeal and pulmonary oedema are more marked. With acetic acid the eschar is pinkish-red and the haemolytic effect is strong: haemoglobinuric nephrosis and acute renal failure, and the smell is a sharp odour of vinegar. With phenol, that is carbolic acid, a carbolic odour comes from the internal organs, and the urine turns greenish-brown on standing in air.

t: Corrosive poisons: alkalis and other substances
n: Corrosive poisons: alkalis and other substances. Alkalis liquefy protein: colliquative, that is, wet, necrosis forms; the damaged area is soft and slippery. Lethal dose: sodium and potassium hydroxide 10–15 g, ammonia solution, that is ammonium hydroxide, 25–40 ml. After absorption into the blood, ammonia solution disturbs the respiratory centre; the danger increases if it is drunk together with alcohol. Other corrosive substances: with formalin the mucous membrane is unchanged, which is fixation, and a characteristic odour comes from the internal organs. With potassium permanganate the eschar is brownish-red, and the lethal dose is 15–20 g. With hydrogen peroxide the mucous membrane is whitish and foamy; if 100 ml of 33% perhydrol is drunk, death is possible. With iodine preparations the eschar is brown, and laryngeal oedema and asphyxia are possible.

Case analysis: corrosive poison. Situation: streaks around the mouth, detached fragments of mucosa in the vomit, severe pain along the oesophagus. These are signs characteristic of a corrosive poison. With an acid there is coagulative, that is, dry, necrosis and a dense brownish-black eschar. With an alkali there is colliquative, that is, wet, necrosis: the area is soft, slippery and greyish-green. The type of acid is inferred from the colour: with sulphuric the mucosa is brownish-black, with nitric it is yellowish. With acetic acid, haemolysis and a sharp smell of vinegar predominate. Attention: an acid is not an alkali. With an acid the mucosa becomes firm and unevenly thickened; with an alkali the stomach wall becomes soft and tears easily.

Destructive poisons: mercury and lead. Pure mercury taken by mouth does not poison, because it does not dissolve. As vapour and in a finely dispersed state, however, it is readily absorbed through the respiratory tract and causes severe poisoning. Corrosive sublimate, that is mercuric dichloride, is a protoplasmic poison: a metallic taste in the mouth, bloody vomiting, oliguria-anuria. Death is most often due to acute renal failure. In the corpse, mercurial stomatitis is found, "sublimate dysentery" in the large intestine, and an enlarged "sublimate kidney", that is toxic necronephrosis. Organic mercury, granosan, is chronic and neurotoxic: a latent period of months, encephalopathy. With lead, the intestinal and renal effects are weaker, while nervous system damage and anaemia are prominent.

Destructive poisons: arsenic and thallium. Arsenic blocks the sulfhydryl groups of enzymes; the capillaries become paralysed, blood pressure falls and collapse occurs. There are two forms of acute poisoning. The gastrointestinal form occurs when it is taken by mouth: vomiting and cholera-like diarrhoea, dehydration, haemorrhagic inflammation; death occurs on day 1–2. The paralytic form occurs with a large dose or parenteral entry: headache, delirium, coma, cerebral oedema, with minimal changes; death occurs in the first hours. In chronic poisoning, dyspepsia, polyneuropathy, hair loss and transverse white lines on the nails are observed. Arsenic persists in hair, nails and bone for years. With thallium, gastroenteritis, alopecia and polyneuropathy occur.

Blood poisons: carbon monoxide. Carbon monoxide enters through the respiratory tract, combines with haemoglobin, and carboxyhaemoglobin is formed. As a result, oxygen transport is impaired and haemic and tissue hypoxia develop. Clinical picture: headache, tinnitus, nausea; then loss of consciousness and convulsive coma. Cadaveric lividity, muscle and liquid blood are pinkish-red; in the internal organs, congestion and petechial haemorrhages are found. The Hoppe-Seyler and Liebmann tests are simple; with rapid death, or after exposure to fresh air, the result may be negative.

Methaemoglobin-forming poisons. Nitrites, nitrate salts, nitrobenzene, aniline, Berthollet's salt and hydroquinone form methaemoglobin; they are used in the manufacture of rubber, dyes and canned goods. In methaemoglobin, trivalent iron, Fe3+, is stably bound to hydroxyl; haemoglobin loses its ability to carry oxygen, and haemic hypoxia develops. At high concentration the resistance of erythrocytes is reduced, and haemolysis, anaemia and methaemoglobinuria occur; nitrates act after being converted to nitrites in the intestine. Cadaveric lividity is bluish-grey or brown, and the blood is brownish; with nitrobenzene there is a bitter almond odour, and with aniline an aromatic odour. After 1–2 days they may not be detectable.

Functional poisons: cyanides and hydrogen sulphide. The cyanide anion binds the iron in cytochrome oxidase: even when there is enough oxygen in the blood, tissue hypoxia and paralysis of the respiratory and cardiac centres develop. With a large dose, consciousness is lost within a minute, followed by convulsions and death. In the corpse there is a bitter almond odour and cherry-coloured patches; the odour is volatile and may disappear quickly. Amygdalin in the kernels of fresh fruit stones, that is apricot, peach and plum, forms hydrocyanic acid in the intestine; the latent period is several hours. Hydrogen sulphide also binds the iron in cytochrome oxidase; at 1% or more in the air, a fulminant form is observed. In the corpse there is a smell of rotten eggs, and the blood and internal organs are cherry-red; hydrogen sulphide accumulates in sewers and mines.

t: Functional poisons: organophosphorus compounds and alcohols
n: Functional poisons: organophosphorus compounds and alcohols. Organophosphorus compounds inhibit the enzyme cholinesterase; acetylcholine accumulates in the tissues. In the corpse, early rigor, constriction of the pupils, foci of spasm in the intestine and excess fluid on the mucous membranes are observed. Ethanol is broken down to acetaldehyde, then to acetic acid and water; acetaldehyde is toxic. Metabolism of alcohols: the metabolite of methyl alcohol is formaldehyde, which is cardio-, nephro- and neurotoxic. The metabolite of ethyl alcohol is acetaldehyde, which causes unpleasant sensations and disturbance of the nervous system. The metabolite of ethylene glycol is oxalic acid, which poisons the liver and kidneys.

Case analysis: functional poison. The case: a 3-year-old girl, after a fall, was unconscious, with convulsions of the body and foam and blood from the mouth; internal bleeding was suspected. When the skull was opened no blood was found, and the girl died; at autopsy, brain swelling and congestion of the pia mater were found. On forensic chemical examination, amidopyrine was found in the stomach and internal organs; it became known that the girl had taken 10 tablets before the fall. Question: why is it dangerous to make a diagnosis relying on a single clinical sign? Which three sources clarify the diagnosis?

Detoxification and chemical-toxicological analysis. For testing blood for alcohol, the skin is not wiped with ethanol; if blood is kept at room temperature for more than a day, up to 1‰ of ethanol may form in it. Detoxification is the neutralisation of the poison and acceleration of its elimination: induced vomiting, gastric lavage, forced diuresis, dialysis, an antidote. Attention: when a strong acid or alkali has been drunk, inducing vomiting is inadvisable; oesophageal damage worsens and burns of the airways are possible. If the poison is known, the objects are taken by the "three points" rule: from where the poison entered, acted and was excreted, that is, the stomach contents, liver and kidneys.

Conclusion and key points. Poisons are divided into those acting mainly locally, that is corrosive, and those acting mainly generally, that is resorptive; the general ones are destructive, blood and functional poisons. Diagnosis is carried out in three stages: the scene and medical documents, examination of the corpse, and laboratory examinations; only all three together justify the conclusion. If the poison is known, samples are taken by the "three points" rule: from where the poison entered, mainly acted and was excreted; if it is unknown, the list is broader. Attention: a forensic chemical result is not proof in itself: a positive result may be due to poison that came from outside, and a negative one to the poison having been excreted or broken down.
